cues.text: Chapter six brings everything together in the AeroFreight capstone integration exercise.
The lab for this session introduces something called CI gate simulation.
CI stands for continuous integration.
The purpose of this exercise is twofold: to avoid merge conflicts, and to avoid rushed secret exposure.
A secret here means something like a password, an API key or a token, the kind of credential that must never end up exposed in code.
Rushed secret exposure is what can happen when people hurry to merge their work and accidentally commit a credential.
The underlying idea is that Agile teams integrate small changes frequently.
Small, frequent integrations are easier to combine, which is how merge conflicts are reduced.
To protect that fast pace, the lab uses a simulated gate.
This gate should fail a commit if lint, security or tests fail.
So there are three checks: lint, which is the check on code style and common mistakes; security, which in this lab is the secret scan; and tests.
If any one of these fails, the commit does not pass.
Now let us look at the code sample, which is written in Python.
Please look at the accompanying code on screen as we go through it.
The code defines a function called gate.
It takes three parameters: lint_ok, secret_scan_ok and tests_ok.
Each one is a true or false value saying whether that check passed.
The function returns the result of calling all on a tuple containing those three values.
The built-in function all returns True only when every item it is given is true.
So the gate passes only if lint passed, the secret scan passed and the tests passed.
If even one is False, the gate returns False.
After the function come two assertions.
The first says assert gate of True, True, True.
All three checks pass, so the gate should return True, and the assertion holds.
The second says assert not gate of True, False, True.
Here lint passes, the secret scan fails, and tests pass.
Because one check failed, the gate returns False, and the word not turns that into True, so this assertion also holds.
In plain terms, the second example shows that a failed secret scan alone is enough to block a commit.
I should be clear that this is simply the code as supplied; I am not claiming here that it was run.
Next, an important qualification.
A simple regex, which is a regular expression pattern used to match text, can catch some hardcoded secrets, but it cannot prove security.
Finding nothing with a simple pattern does not mean the code is safe.
For that reason, in production you should use real linters, real secret scanners and real test tools, rather than relying on a home-made pattern like the one in a lab simulation.
The source also gives security practices for when things go wrong.
Revoke exposed credentials, meaning that if a secret has been exposed, it should be cancelled so it can no longer be used.
And never log secrets, so that credentials do not leak into log files.
Finally, the source describes the Agile workflow in order.
First, implement the story.
Second, review.
Third, run the gates.
Fourth, integrate.
Fifth, demo the working increment.
And sixth, retrospect, which means the team reflects on how it worked and what to improve.
Notice where the gates sit: after review and before integration, so only changes that pass are merged.
And the closing principle is this: quality is not postponed to a final sprint.
Quality checks happen throughout, on every change, rather than being left until the end of the project.
